title.narrative: Inventorying and safeguarding Yazidi intangible cultural heritage, Iraq

description.narrative: The Yazidi Genocide was perpetrated by the so-called Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (Daesh) between 2014 and 2017. During this period, Daesh committed acts amounting to genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, including mass executions, forced religious conversions to Islam, enslavement and widespread sexual violence against women and girls. Daesh forcibly transferred thousands of captured Yazidis into Syria where girls as young as nine were subjected to sexual slavery and Yazidi boys as young as seven were coerced into military training and deployed in combat and suicide operations. The Yazidi community in Iraq continues to bear the deep scars of the Islamic State’s occupation, during which both lives and cultural identity were targeted through the destruction of shrines, sacred artifacts and traditions. In response, UNESCO Iraq, in collaboration with the Nadia Initiative and the Lalish Cultural Centre, is stepping up its efforts to inventory Yazidi intangible cultural heritage (ICH). Building on a 2023 survey of 97 shrines and 88 related practices, the current project focuses on documenting the non-religious aspects of Yazidi ICH, with the aim of creating a searchable online database that is accessible to the community, particularly young people. The outcomes will include strengthened identity, continuity and social cohesion, and the activities will focus on research, documentation and digital tools to safeguard and revitalise Yazidi heritage. The project aims to safeguard and promote the Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) of the Yazidi community by strengthening local capacities for community-based inventorying and documentation. Through systematic training, participatory workshops, and mentoring by international experts, 34 field team members and 9 representatives of the Yazidi community will develop the skills required to identify, document, and manage Yazidi ICH. It is envisaged thatmore than 150 ICH elements will be inventoried and validated through community engagement and intergenerational participation, with at least 25 young people actively contributing to the process. The project will result in a comprehensive digital database, a finalised, quality-assured inventory of ICH and a published volume showcasing documented Yazidi cultural expressions. The framework also ensures continuous monitoring, quality assurance and stakeholder involvement, thereby fostering social cohesion, strengthening cultural identity, and supporting the transmission of heritage knowledge to younger generations.
